title: Blind, not wicked
hookLine: would you be angry with a blind man? then pity the one blind about good and bad (Discourses 1.18)

lines: A HARD BUMP IN THE AISLE.
WHAT IF YOU SAW EVERYONE THAT WAY?
cards: Someone bumps your cart hard in the grocery store and keeps walking. You turn, ready to say something, and see the white cane. The bump was exactly as hard as it was a second ago, and your shin stings just the same.
The only thing that's different is what you now understand about the person. Epictetus asks: what if you understood everyone who wrongs you that way?

teach.h: EVERYONE REACHES FOR WHAT SEEMS GOOD.
teach.b: Discourses book one, chapter eighteen: that we ought not to be angry with the mistakes of others. Epictetus, the Stoic teacher, starts from something he thinks is true of all of us.
Every person agrees with what seems true to them and reaches for what seems good to them. No one does wrong while thinking, this is bad for me, and I want it anyway.
So when someone steals or cheats, they've misjudged. They think the stolen thing is good for them, and they're wrong about what's good. That's the whole diagnosis.
His students push back. But they're thieves! Robbers!
Shouldn't such a person be put to death? Then say it accurately, Epictetus answers.

teach.h: BLIND IN JUDGMENT, NOT IN EYES.
teach.b: Shouldn't this person, deceived about the most important things, blind, not in the eyes that tell white from black, but in the judgment that tells good from bad, be put to death?
Say it that way, and you'll hear how harsh it is. You wouldn't punish the blind or the deaf for not seeing or hearing.
Pity them instead. Show them the mistake, and you may see them stop. This doesn't mean pretending harm didn't happen, or that no one should be held to account.
Epictetus is talking about anger, the heat inside you.
His claim is that the heat rests on a picture of the other person as wicked by choice, and that the picture is usually wrong.

how: Some Stoic practitioners reframe a person who has wronged them as mistaken about what is good, which can soften anger without excusing the harm.

o: unable to see, and so owed special care in public
too angry to think clearly about what happened
unable to judge good from bad, not wicked by choice

games.q: blind, not wicked: tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says no one should ever be held to account
his target is anger, the heat inside us, not accountability.
he says no one does wrong while seeing it as bad for themselves
everyone reaches for what seems good to them.
Epictetus compares the wrongdoer to someone blind or deaf
blind not in the eyes, but in the judgment that tells good from bad.

games.q: your students say: shouldn't this robber be put to death? you're Epictetus. what do you say?
o: say it accurately: shouldn't this person, blind about good and bad, be punished? hear how harsh it is.
games.why: he has them restate it as punishing someone blind in judgment, so they can hear the harshness, and says to pity such people instead.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has annoyed you lately, not the worst person in your life, and picture what they did. Ask what they thought was good when they did it: comfort, safety, being right, getting ahead?
See them reaching for it and missing, and notice whether the heat in your chest shifts, even a little, toward pity; if it doesn't, that's all right.

wordCard.voice: Blind. Epictetus' word for the wrongdoer: not wicked by choice, but blind in the judgment that tells good from bad, and owed pity more than anger.

orig.note: Greek typhlos: blind; Epictetus uses blindness for the judgment that can't tell good from bad.

carryVoice: Your line: pity them instead. Anger pictures wickedness; Epictetus sees a misjudgment. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.18 (that we ought not to be angry with the errors of others)
